text: When a matrix transforms the plane, almost every arrow is knocked off its line: it turns to point somewhere new as well as changing length. For many matrices, though, a few special directions survive, where an arrow stays on its own line and is only stretched or squeezed. Those are the eigenvectors, and they are often the clearest way to understand what a matrix does.

Here is a matrix acting on a fan of arrows. As the plane moves, most of them swing round to new directions. The arrows along the horizontal axis, however, stay on that axis and come out three times longer, and the arrows along one diagonal stay on their diagonal and come out twice as long.

Written as an equation, the matrix A times v equals lambda times v. On the left, the matrix does its full work, turning included; on the right, only a scalar acts, which can stretch or flip an arrow but never turn it. The number lambda is called the eigenvalue, the stretch factor, and the word eigen is German for own, because these directions belong to the matrix itself.

To find them, move everything to one side: A minus lambda times the identity, applied to v, gives zero. A nonzero arrow is being sent to zero, so this new matrix must crush the plane flat, and from the lesson on determinants, that means its determinant is zero. Solving that equation gives the eigenvalues, and each eigenvalue then gives its own line of eigenvectors.

Not every matrix has real eigenvectors. A rotation by a quarter turn moves every arrow off its line, so none survives, and the equation for lambda has no real solution. A shear keeps just one direction, the line it slides along, while every other arrow leans over.

So why do eigenvectors matter? Apply the same matrix again and again, and almost any arrow you start with is pulled towards the direction with the largest eigenvalue, because that component is multiplied by the biggest factor at every step and soon dominates the rest. This repeated multiplication is called power iteration. It finds the leading eigenvector without solving any equation, and it is how the original PageRank algorithm ranked pages on the web.

Repeated multiplication is also what happens to a signal passed through many layers of a deep network, or through many steps of an old recurrent network. When the important stretch factors are larger than one, values explode; when they are smaller than one, the signal fades away, which is one reason those recurrent networks forgot the start of long sentences. Next comes the singular value decomposition, which finds the stretching directions of every matrix, even one with no eigenvectors at all.
